name: Abinoam (Barak's father)
title: Father of the judge Barak
summary: Abinoam is known from the Book of Judges as the father of Barak, the military leader from Kedesh in Naphtali who liberated Israel from Canaanite oppression. The name Abinoam means 'my father is grace' and reflects a Semitic naming tradition where positive traits were woven into family identity. Although Scripture tells us nothing about Abinoam's own deeds, his name lives on through the patronymic 'Barak son of Abinoam'. The family lived in Kedesh in Naphtali, a Levitical city of refuge strategically located in northern Israel near the border with Canaanite territory.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as Barak's father
keyEvents.description: Abinoam is mentioned as the father of Barak when the prophetess Deborah calls Barak to gather an army against Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite forces. Barak lived in Kedesh in Naphtali.

keyEvents.title: Barak's victory over Sisera
keyEvents.description: Abinoam's son Barak led Israel's army to a decisive victory over Sisera's forces at the Kishon River. Throughout the account, Barak is identified by his patronymic 'son of Abinoam'.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Deborah's Song of Victory
keyEvents.description: In the song of victory that Deborah and Barak sang after their triumph over Sisera, Barak is identified as the son of Abinoam. The song is considered among the oldest poetic texts in the Hebrew Bible.

versions.summary: Abinoam was the father of Barak, the Israelite military commander who, together with the prophetess Deborah, defeated Sisera, the Canaanite army leader. Although little is known about Abinoam himself, his name is preserved in the Bible through his famous son who liberated Israel from Canaanite oppression.
versions.title: Father of one of Israel's judges
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'patriarch' can be somewhat misleading. The term 'patriarch' is traditionally used for the fathers of Israel (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). A more precise role for Abinoam would be 'father' or 'tribal chief', possibly supplemented with 'Israelite from Naphtali'.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could mention that the name Abinoam means 'my father is grace/goodness', which provides linguistic context.; [minor] In the second key event ('Barak's victory over Sisera'), strictly speaking, there is an event connected to Barak, not directly to Abinoam. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to include it for context, but it should be clarified that Abinoam is only mentioned indirectly.; [major] There are no footnotes covering historical, linguistic, or theological details. The name Abinoam, the place Kedesh in Naphtali, and the historical context of Canaanite oppression deserve footnotes.

versions.summary: Abinoam was the father of Barak, the Israelite military commander who, together with the prophetess Deborah, defeated the Canaanite general Sisera. The name Abinoam means 'my father is grace' and testifies to a pious naming tradition in Israel. Although little is known about Abinoam himself, his name is preserved in Scripture through his famous son, who liberated Israel from Canaanite oppression. The family lived in Kedesh in Naphtali, a strategically important city in northern Israel.
versions.title: Father of the judge Barak
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (begins with exactly the same sentence: 'Abinoam was the father of Barak, the Israelite commander who together with the prophetess Deborah defeated the Canaanite commander Sisera.' It should be rephrased more distinctly to set it apart from the previous version.; [minor] The title 'Barak's Victory over Sisera' is good, but the description mentions 'iron chariots' – the text in Judg 4:13 refers to 900 iron chariots, while verses 12–16, which are referenced here, primarily cover the battle itself. This is correct, but verse 13 could be included to support the mention of iron chariots.; [minor] The description states that Deborah's song 'is considered one of the oldest poetic texts in the Old Testament.' Although this is a common academic assessment, it should be phrased more neutrally, for example: 'The song is counted among the oldest poetic texts in the Hebrew Bible.'; [minor] The footnote says that the name type testifies that 'parents expressed gratitude to God through their children's names,' but the name Abinoam refers to 'my father' (avi), not directly to God. It is more precise to say this is a theophoric or familial expression praising a quality (grace/goodness), possibly with reference to God as the divine Father.

footnotes.text: The name Abinoam (Hebrew: אֲבִינֹעַם) is composed of 'avi' (my father) and 'noam' (grace, beauty, goodness), meaning 'my father is grace'. The element 'avi' can be understood either as a reference to a human father or as an image of God as Father. This type of name is known from several Semitic cultures and testifies to a tradition where positive qualities were linked to the identity of the family line.

Kedesh in Naphtali, the home of Barak's family, is identified with Tell Qades in Upper Galilee. The city was one of the Levitical cities of refuge (Josh 20:7) and was strategically located near the border between Israelite and Canaanite territory. Archaeological excavations have uncovered settlement traces from the Bronze Age at the site.

The Canaanite oppression that affected Barak's family and the tribal region of Naphtali was linked to Jabin, king of Hazor, and his general Sisera. Archaeological excavations at Tel Hazor have revealed a significant destruction layer from around the 12th century BC, which several scholars associate with the events in Judges 4–5.

In rabbinic tradition, individuals who are primarily known through their descendants are still regarded as highly significant because they are considered to have passed on faith and values. That Barak rose up as Israel's military commander was seen as indirect testimony to his father's piety and upbringing.

Deborah's song in Judges 5 is considered by many scholars to be one of the oldest preserved poetic texts in the Hebrew Bible. The archaic language form and the detailed geographical and tribal descriptions suggest that the song may have originated close to the time of the events.
